takeaways: A bus replaces n(n − 1)/2 point-to-point links with one shared pair; the price is that bandwidth, latency, determinism and bus load become design limits.
Describe any network by topology, organization, access method, OSI layers and class; vehicle buses define only layers 1 and 2 and leave transport and application to other standards.
In CAN the dominant 0 wins, so the lowest identifier wins arbitration with no lost bits; an 8-byte frame takes 222 to 270 µs at 500 kbit/s.
CAN FD keeps arbitration and speeds up only the data phase, carrying up to 64 bytes; a classic node cannot stay on an FD bus.
LIN is cheap and polled, FlexRay is time-triggered on two channels, and Ethernet is switched and fast; each fills a cost, speed and timing niche.
MOST carries media in a ring clocked by a timing master at 44.1 or 48 kHz; streams take fixed bytes in every frame.
The central gateway routes, repacks, filters and times signals between all buses and the OBD socket, and every crossing adds delay.
OBD-II fixes the socket, services, PIDs and DTC format; scale every PID with its formula and remember the two-trip rule for the MIL.
MISRA C makes the code analysable; ISO 26262 turns hazards into ASILs, safety goals and evidence; neither replaces the other.
V2X, VANET routing and DSRC timing are all numbers questions: warning distance, contact time, greedy distances and BSM airtime.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the bus systems with a neat diagram: the CAN frame and arbitration, LIN, FlexRay and MOST, and how networks are coupled through a gateway. Expect a short calculation inside the long answer (frame time, bus load, an arbitration trace or an OBD-II decode), and draw the topology or the layer stack in every answer.

bank.q: Explain why modern vehicles exchange data over buses instead of point-to-point wiring. Describe cross-system functions and the requirements a vehicle bus system must meet, with a calculation.
outline: Point-to-point links grow as n(n − 1)/2
Bus: one shared pair, one transceiver per ECU, numbered messages
Cross-system functions: traction control, shared wheel speed, gear-shift torque dip, crash unlock
Domains and the gateway
Requirements: data rate, latency, determinism, reliability, fault tolerance, EMC, cost, sleep and wake, expandability, diagnosis
Bus load U = Σ(bits ÷ period) ÷ bit rate with a margin
answer: Definitions. An ECU (electronic control unit) is a small computer that reads sensors and drives actuators. A signal is one quantity (engine speed); a message or frame is one packet on a bus that carries several signals. In point-to-point wiring each signal has its own wire from the unit that measures it to every unit that uses it; on a serial data bus the measuring unit sends the value once and every unit that needs it reads it (multiplexing).

answer.text: Why point-to-point wiring fails. To join n units directly to each other needs L = n(n − 1)/2 links, each with a driver at both ends. A bus needs one twisted pair and one transceiver per unit:

answer: So with 10 ECUs the bus saves 45 − 1 = 44 cable runs and 90 − 10 = 80 driver circuits. Fewer wires mean a lighter, cheaper harness with fewer connectors to corrode, and a new unit can be added by tapping the existing pair. Draw the two sketches: a hexagon of six ECUs with 15 crossing lines, and the same six ECUs hanging from one pair with a 120 Ω terminator at each end.

Cross-system functions. Many features need more than one ECU, and only a network makes them practical: (a) traction control, where the ABS ECU sees a spinning wheel and asks the engine ECU to cut torque; (b) wheel speed measured once by the ABS ECU and used by the speedometer, navigation, electric power steering and gearbox; (c) a torque dip requested by the gearbox ECU during each shift; (d) crash unlock, where the airbag ECU tells the body ECU to unlock the doors and flash the hazard lamps; (e) adaptive cruise, where the radar ECU commands engine torque and brake pressure.

Domains. ECUs are grouped into powertrain, chassis, body and comfort, infotainment and diagnostics; each domain gets a bus suited to it, and a gateway joins them and forwards only the messages that must cross.

Requirements for a bus system: (1) data rate, from about 20 kbit/s for doors to 100 Mbit/s for cameras; (2) latency, the delay from send to receive; (3) determinism, a guaranteed worst case, needed by brakes and steering; (4) reliability: CRC, acknowledgement and fault confinement so one bad node cannot block the bus; (5) fault tolerance after a broken wire; (6) electromagnetic compatibility; (7) low cost per node; (8) sleep and wake-up so a parked car draws little current; (9) expandability; (10) diagnostic access from the workshop socket.

answer.text: Bus load calculation. A 500 kbit/s powertrain bus carries 25 messages of 125 bits, each every 10 ms:

answer: 62.5 per cent is inside a design limit of about 70 per cent but leaves little room. Adding five more such messages gives 30 × 125 ÷ 0.010 = 375 000 bit/s, U = 75 per cent, over the limit, so the designer would lengthen some periods, move messages to another bus or use CAN FD.

Check and conclusion. 12 × 11/2 = 66 and 25 × 125 = 3125 bits per 10 ms agree with the figures above. A bus trades a heavy harness for a shared resource, so its rate, latency, determinism and load must be designed, and the gateway keeps the domains apart.

bank.q: Describe the network topologies used in vehicles, the organization and control mechanisms of a vehicle network, the OSI reference model as it applies to CAN, and the classification of bus systems.
outline: Bus, star, ring, daisy chain, hybrid with the effect of a broken cable
Master-slave and multi-master; client-server and producer-consumer
Addressing: subscriber, message and transmission oriented
Access: master polling, TDMA, token, CSMA/CD versus CAN's bit-wise arbitration
Seven OSI layers; CAN covers 1 and 2; ISO-TP at layer 4; UDS and OBD at layer 7
SAE classes A, B, C and the higher class with examples

answer.text: Topology is the wiring shape. Sketch each and state its fault behaviour:

head: Topology
Wiring
One broken cable
Example
rows: trunk break usually stops the bus; stub break loses one node
each node to a hub or switch
loses one node; hub is a single point of failure
each node to the next, closed
single ring stops; double ring survives

answer: Network organization says who may start a transfer: master-slave (one master starts every exchange, as in LIN) or multi-master (any node may start, as in CAN). In software, the tester and an ECU follow a client-server pattern, while periodic signals follow a producer-consumer pattern: one node broadcasts and every interested node takes the value.

Addressing: subscriber-oriented (the message carries the receiver's address), message-oriented (the identifier names the content and receivers filter, as in CAN) and transmission-oriented (the time slot identifies the message, as in FlexRay's static segment).

Control mechanisms (bus access): centralised deterministic access by master polling (LIN); decentralised deterministic access by TDMA (FlexRay static segment) or token passing; random access by CSMA. In CSMA/CD, as in early office Ethernet, a collision destroys both frames and both retry. CAN settles the collision bit by bit, so the higher-priority frame survives (often called CSMA/CR).

answer.text: OSI reference model applied to CAN (draw it as a stack):
Worked transport-layer example: a 34-byte diagnostic reply on classic CAN.
answer.pre:
first frame: 6 bytes  → 34 − 6 = 28 left
consecutive frames: 28 ÷ 7 = 4 frames of 7 bytes
frames sent by the ECU = 1 + 4 = 5   (6 + 4 × 7 = 34 ✓)

answer.text: Classification of bus systems:

answer: Buses are also classed by application (diagnostics, safety, multimedia, x-by-wire). Examples to quote: a door module sending 8 frames of 100 bits every 100 ms needs 8 kbit/s, Class A; engine and gearbox traffic of 187.5 kbit/s is Class C; an uncompressed 640 × 480, 16-bit, 30 frame/s camera needs 147.5 Mbit/s, the multimedia class.

Check: the ISO-TP count 6 + 28 = 34 bytes and the class bands agree with the rates quoted; a vehicle network is therefore a hybrid topology of Class A to D buses joined by gateways, each bus defining only OSI layers 1 and 2.

bank.q: Describe the CAN data frame field by field and explain bit-wise arbitration, bit stuffing and error handling. Calculate the length and duration of an 8-byte frame at 500 kbit/s. How does CAN FD differ?
outline: Physical layer: CAN_H and CAN_L, dominant and recessive levels, 120 Ω terminations
Frame: SOF, identifier, RTR, IDE, r0, DLC, data, CRC, ACK, EOF, interframe space
Wired-AND arbitration, lowest identifier wins, non-destructive
Bit stuffing after five equal bits
Five error types, error frame, TEC and REC limits, bus-off
Frame length 111 bits, worst case 135; 222 to 270 µs
CAN FD: RRS, FDF, BRS, ESI, DLC codes to 64 bytes, longer CRC
answer: Physical layer. Each node has a controller and a transceiver on a twisted pair, CAN_H and CAN_L, terminated by 120 Ω at each end (60 Ω measured across the pair). Recessive (logic 1): both wires about 2.5 V. Dominant (logic 0): CAN_H about 3.5 V, CAN_L about 1.5 V. A dominant bit from any node overrides recessive bits from all others (wired-AND).

answer.text: Frame fields (draw them as a strip):

head: Field
Bits
Job
rows: dominant start bit; synchronises all nodes
receivers that found the frame correct drive the slot dominant

answer: Arbitration. All waiting nodes send SOF together and then their identifiers, most significant bit first, reading the bus after each bit. A node that sends recessive 1 but reads dominant 0 has lost; it stops at once and becomes a receiver. Example: 0x123 (001 0010 0011) against 0x121 (001 0010 0001): the bits agree down to bit 2; at bit 1, 0x123 sends 1 and 0x121 sends 0, so 0x121 wins. Because nothing of the winner is damaged, the scheme is non-destructive and the lowest identifier has the highest priority.
Bit stuffing. After five equal bits the transmitter adds one opposite bit, from SOF to the end of the CRC; receivers remove it. This keeps edges for resynchronisation.

Error handling. Each node checks for bit, stuff, CRC, form and ACK errors. On an error it sends an error frame of six dominant bits; all nodes discard the frame and the sender repeats it. Error counters (TEC, REC) rise on errors and fall on good frames: error active up to 127, error passive above 127, bus-off when TEC exceeds 255. This fault confinement stops a faulty node from blocking the bus.

answer.text: Frame length and duration for 8 data bytes at 500 kbit/s:
answer.pre:
fixed bits SOF..EOF = 1+11+1+1+1+4+15+1+1+1+7 = 44
with data:       44 + 64 = 108 bits;  + 3 IFS = 111 bits
stuffed region   1+11+1+1+1+4+64+15 = 98 bits
worst stuffing   (98 − 1) ÷ 4 = 24.25 → 24 bits  → 135 bits
bit time         1 ÷ 500 000 = 2 µs
duration         111 × 2 = 222 µs ;  135 × 2 = 270 µs
data efficiency  64 ÷ 111 = 57.7 %

answer: CAN FD. Arbitration and ACK stay the same. The RTR position becomes RRS (always dominant, no remote frames); then FDF (recessive: FD format), a reserved bit, BRS (recessive: switch the data phase to the fast rate, for example 2 Mbit/s) and ESI (error state of the sender). DLC 9 to 15 codes 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 48 and 64 bytes. The CRC is 17 bits up to 16 bytes and 21 bits above. Classic controllers cannot share an FD bus, because they see the recessive FDF bit as a form error and destroy the frame.
Check: 108 bits from SOF to EOF plus the 3-bit gap gives 111; at 2 µs a bit, 222 µs, so a fully loaded 500 kbit/s bus could carry at most about 4500 such frames per second.

bank.q: Compare LIN, FlexRay and automotive Ethernet on topology, data rate, access method, determinism and typical use, with a frame-time calculation for LIN.
outline: LIN: one wire, master and up to 15 slaves, 1 to 20 kbit/s, schedule table, header and response
LIN frame: break, sync, PID with parity, data, checksum; T = (34 + 10(n + 1))τ, Tₘₐₓ = 1.4T
FlexRay: two channels at 10 Mbit/s, bus or star, static TDMA and dynamic minislots, symbol window, NIT
Ethernet: 100BASE-T1 and 1000BASE-T1 on one pair, switched star, VLAN, SOME/IP, TSN, 10BASE-T1S
Comparison table and where each is used
answer: LIN. One signal wire and ground at battery voltage; a master and up to 15 slaves at 1 to 20 kbit/s (often 19.2 kbit/s). The master's schedule table fixes which frame is sent in each slot. For each slot the master sends a header (break of at least 13 dominant bits, sync byte 0x55, protected identifier of 6 ID bits plus 2 parity bits) and the publishing node sends the response (1 to 8 data bytes and a checksum). No arbitration is needed because only the master starts frames.

answer.text: LIN frame time for 2 and 8 data bytes at 19.2 kbit/s (τ = 52.08 µs):

answer: So a 10 ms slot is enough even for the longest frame, and a schedule of five 10 ms slots repeats each frame every 50 ms.

FlexRay. Two independent channels, A and B, each 10 Mbit/s, wired as a bus, an active star or a mix. Time is split into communication cycles (typically 1 to 5 ms): a static segment of equal slots, each owned by one node (TDMA); a dynamic segment of minislots in which a node with data stretches its slot (FTDMA, lower numbers first); a symbol window for symbols such as CAS and MTS; and network idle time for clock correction. A static message has a worst-case delay of one cycle and can be sent on both channels for redundancy.

Automotive Ethernet. 100BASE-T1 (100 Mbit/s) and 1000BASE-T1 (1 Gbit/s) send full duplex over one unshielded twisted pair, so the harness is light; office Ethernet needs two pairs (100BASE-TX) or four (1000BASE-T). Each link joins two devices, so the network is a star of switches with no collisions. VLANs separate traffic, SOME/IP gives service calls, DoIP speeds diagnostics, and AVB/TSN adds time sync and scheduled traffic for bounded delay. 10BASE-T1S lets several nodes share one short pair.

answer.text: Comparison:

head: LIN
FlexRay
Ethernet
rows: switched star, one pair per link

answer.text: Time to move a 1000-byte block (8000 bits), ignoring overhead:
answer.pre:
LIN 19.2 kbit/s:  8000 ÷ 19 200 = 416.7 ms
FlexRay 10 Mbit/s: 8000 ÷ 10⁷   = 0.8 ms
Ethernet 100 Mbit/s: 8000 ÷ 10⁸ = 80 µs

answer: Conclusion: the three are not rivals but layers of one network. LIN keeps cheap modules off CAN, FlexRay gives guaranteed timing for x-by-wire, and Ethernet carries bulk data; gateways join them. Check: 124 bits at 52.08 µs is 6.458 ms, and 416.7 ms ÷ 0.08 ms ≈ 5200 times between LIN and Ethernet.

bank.q: Explain the MOST bus: its topology, the role of the timing master, the frame structure and its channels. Then explain how the networks of a car are coupled through gateways, with an example of a networked vehicle.
outline: MOST ring of up to 64 devices, plastic optical fibre, red LED; MOST50 and MOST150 also on copper
Timing master sends frames at 44.1 or 48 kHz; slaves recover the clock
MOST25 frame 64 bytes: 60 data bytes split synchronous and asynchronous, 2 control bytes
Channel rates from bytes per frame × 8 × f
Repeater, bridge, router, gateway by OSI layer
Central gateway jobs and crossing delay
Example vehicle network
answer: MOST (Media Oriented Systems Transport) is a bus for infotainment: audio, video, navigation and phone. Up to 64 devices form a ring; each receives from the previous device and sends to the next. MOST25 uses plastic optical fibre with a 1 mm core and a red LED, which is light, cheap and immune to electrical noise; MOST50 and MOST150 can also use copper. Draw a ring of head unit, amplifier, navigation and rear display with arrows in one direction.

Timing master. One device, usually the head unit, sends frames continuously at the system frequency, 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz. All other devices are timing slaves: they recover the clock from the frames, take out their bytes, insert their own and pass the frame on. So every stream is locked to one clock and audio arrives one sample per frame without buffering. A single broken fibre stops the ring, so MOST has a ring break diagnosis.

Frame and channels (MOST25). One frame is 64 bytes = 512 bits: a header byte, 60 data bytes, 2 control bytes and a trailer byte. The boundary descriptor splits the 60 data bytes into a synchronous channel (byte positions reserved for each stream, such as 4 bytes for 16-bit stereo audio) and an asynchronous channel for packet data such as map tiles. The 2 control bytes form the control channel for commands and status; a control message is spread over 16 frames.

answer.text: Channel budget at 44.1 kHz with a stereo radio stream and a mono navigation voice:
answer.pre:
gross rate       64 × 8 × 44 100 = 22.58 Mbit/s (about 23 Mbit/s)
stereo 16-bit    2 × 2 bytes = 4 bytes/frame → 4 × 8 × 44 100 = 1.411 Mbit/s
mono 16-bit      2 bytes/frame → 705.6 kbit/s
synchronous used 4 + 2 = 6 bytes; asynchronous left 60 − 6 = 54 bytes
asynchronous     54 × 8 × 44 100 = 19.05 Mbit/s
control channel  2 × 8 × 44 100 = 705.6 kbit/s

answer: MOST50 uses 1024-bit frames and MOST150 3072-bit frames (about 150 Mbit/s at 48 kHz, with an Ethernet channel).

Coupling of networks, by OSI layer: a repeater (layer 1) regenerates the signal; a bridge (layer 2) joins segments of one protocol; a router (layer 3) chooses paths between networks; a gateway (up to layer 7) joins different protocols, rates and formats. Car buses differ, so they are coupled by gateways, usually one central gateway.

Gateway jobs: (1) message routing by an identifier table; (2) signal routing, unpacking signals and repacking them into new frames; (3) rate adaptation and buffering between fast and slow buses; (4) filtering, so infotainment can never send chassis frames; (5) diagnostic routing from the OBD socket to every ECU; (6) network management, waking and sleeping the buses.

answer.text: Crossing delay, 111-bit frame from 500 kbit/s powertrain CAN to 125 kbit/s body CAN with 0.20 ms processing:

answer: Example of a networked vehicle: powertrain CAN at 500 kbit/s (engine, gearbox), chassis CAN or FlexRay (ABS and ESP, steering, suspension), body CAN at 125 kbit/s with LIN sub-buses (doors, seats, climate), a MOST ring or Ethernet for infotainment, and the OBD socket, all on the central gateway. Draw this star of buses round the gateway with the MOST ring on one side. Check: 6 + 54 = 60 data bytes, and 0.222 + 0.888 + 0.20 = 1.31 ms.

bank.q: Explain the OBD-II system: the connector and its pins, the communication protocols, the diagnostic services and PIDs, the DTC format, the readiness monitors and the MIL. Decode an engine-speed reply.
outline: Emissions law; J1962 16-pin socket within reach of the driver
Five protocols; CAN with 11- or 29-bit IDs at 250 or 500 kbit/s
Services 01 to 0A; PIDs and scaling
DTC: letter, generic or maker digit, subsystem, fault number; two-byte coding
Monitors, drive cycle, pending code, two-trip rule, MIL, clearing
answer: Purpose. OBD-II is an emissions-diagnostics standard: one socket, one set of messages and one code format, so any scan tool can read any compliant car. It became law for petrol cars in the USA from 1996 and in Europe as EOBD from 2001; in India BS-VI Phase 2 (April 2023) brought full OBD-II monitoring.

answer.text: Connector (SAE J1962): 16 pins in two rows of eight, within reach of the driver. Draw it with these pins labelled:

answer: Protocols. Five were allowed: SAE J1850 PWM and VPW, ISO 9141-2, ISO 14230 (KWP2000) and ISO 15765-4 (CAN). CAN is required on US cars from model year 2008, with 11-bit or 29-bit identifiers at 500 or 250 kbit/s (most cars: 11-bit, 500 kbit/s).

answer.text: Services (the reply carries the service number + 0x40):

answer: PIDs. Each live value has a parameter identifier and a scaling formula: PID 04 load = A × 100 ÷ 255 %, PID 05 coolant = A − 40 °C, PID 0C speed = (256A + B) ÷ 4 rpm, PID 0D vehicle speed = A km/h.

answer.text: Decode: request 01 0C, reply 41 0C 0C 80.

answer: DTC format. A letter and four digits: P powertrain, C chassis, B body, U network; first digit 0 generic, 1 maker-specific; for P codes the second digit is the subsystem (3 ignition and misfire) and the last two the fault. P0301 is a generic misfire in cylinder 1. On the bus a DTC is two bytes: the top 2 bits give the letter, the next 2 the first digit, then three 4-bit digits; bytes 03 01 decode to P0301.

Monitors and lamp. Continuous monitors (misfire, fuel system, components) and non-continuous ones (catalyst, oxygen sensor and heater, evaporative system, EGR) run during a drive cycle; readiness status shows which have completed. A first failure stores a pending code (service 07). If the fault returns in the next drive cycle (two-trip rule), the code is confirmed, a freeze frame is stored and the MIL comes on; a catalyst-damaging misfire flashes it at once. Three good drive cycles turn the lamp off. Service 04 clears codes and resets readiness, but an unrepaired fault returns, and permanent codes (0A) stay until the monitor passes.
Check: 0x0C80 = 3200 and 3200 ÷ 4 = 800 rpm; the pin list has ground (4, 5), power (16) and CAN (6, 14) as the examiner expects.

bank.q: Explain how ISO 26262 assigns an ASIL and what the safety lifecycle demands, and how MISRA C supports it. Include an ASIL determination and an FTTI budget.
outline: Item definition, HARA, severity, exposure and controllability
ASIL A to D and QM; the S + E + C rule for the table
Safety goals, safety concept, safety mechanisms, safe state, decomposition
FTTI and its budget
Hardware metrics SPFM and LFM
V-model, verification and confirmation
MISRA C categories, rules and deviations as software evidence
answer: Scope. ISO 26262:2018 is the functional-safety standard for road vehicles, in 12 parts, organised as a V-model: requirements on the left, implementation at the bottom, verification and validation on the right. Draw the V with item definition and HARA at the top left and the safety validation at the top right.

Item definition fixes the boundary: which ECUs, sensors, actuators and functions are inside. HARA (hazard analysis and risk assessment) lists hazardous events and rates each for severity S0 to S3, exposure E0 to E4 and controllability C0 to C3.

answer.text: ASIL determination. For S1–S3, E1–E4 and C1–C3, the standard's table equals the rule: S + E + C = 10 → D, 9 → C, 8 → B, 7 → A, 6 or less → QM.

head: Hazard
S
E
C
Sum
ASIL
rows: Loss of brake assist at low speed

answer: Safety goals and concept. Each hazardous event gets a safety goal with its ASIL, for example "no unintended steering torque" (ASIL D). The functional and technical safety concepts assign safety mechanisms: plausibility checks between two sensors, watchdogs, end-to-end protection of bus messages, redundancy, and a safe state. ASIL decomposition may split a requirement into two independent ones, for example B(D) + B(D), if independence is proved.

answer.text: FTTI budget. The fault tolerant time interval is the minimum time from a fault to a possible hazard. Example: FTTI = 200 ms, sampling 20 ms, confirmation 40 ms, actuator 30 ms.
answer.pre:
detection time = 200 − (20 + 40 + 30) = 200 − 90 = 110 ms
fault flagged by 20 + 40 + 110 = 170 ms
safe state reached by 170 + 30 = 200 ms = FTTI ✓

answer.text: Hardware metrics. SPFM = 1 − (λ<sub>SPF</sub> + λ<sub>RF</sub>) ÷ λ, computed from failure rates and the diagnostic coverage of the safety mechanisms; ASIL D needs at least 99 per cent. Example: λ = 200 FIT, λ<sub>SPF</sub> = 0.5 FIT, λ<sub>RF</sub> = 1.0 FIT.

answer: The latent fault metric (LFM) checks faults that stay hidden until a second fault occurs. Verification includes reviews, tests, fault injection and, for higher ASILs, independent confirmation measures and a safety assessment; the result is a safety case.

MISRA C supports part 6 (software). Its guidelines are mandatory, required or advisory; a required rule may be broken only by a documented deviation. Typical rules: no recursion, no malloc or free (Rule 21.3), no value-losing implicit conversion, braces on every body, pointer arithmetic only within arrays, check error returns. A static analyser checks the code. MISRA makes the code predictable and analysable, but it is only one piece of evidence: without HARA, safety goals, metrics and verification there is no ISO 26262 compliance.
Check: 3 + 4 + 3 = 10 gives D, and 20 + 40 + 110 + 30 = 200 ms fills the FTTI exactly.

bank.q: Three nodes start sending standard CAN data frames with identifiers 0x123, 0x0F1 and 0x2A0 at the same instant on a 500 kbit/s bus. Trace the arbitration bit by bit, name the winner, and state when each frame finishes if all carry 8 data bytes and no stuff bits are needed.
outline: Convert to 11-bit binary, MSB first
Compare bit by bit; recessive sender that reads dominant drops out
0x2A0 drops at bit 9, 0x123 at bit 8; 0x0F1 wins
Losers compete again after the frame: 0x123 then 0x2A0
Frame time 111 bits × 2 µs = 222 µs; finish times 222, 444, 666 µs
No data lost; identifier is priority
answer: Rule. During arbitration each node sends its identifier most significant bit first and reads the bus; dominant 0 overrides recessive 1; a node that sent 1 and reads 0 stops and becomes a receiver. The lowest identifier therefore wins.

answer.text: Identifiers in decimal and 11-bit binary:
Bit-by-bit trace ("–" means the node has stopped sending):

head: Bit
X 0x123
Y 0x0F1
Z 0x2A0
Bus
Event
rows: Z sent 1, read 0: Z drops out
X sent 1, read 0: X drops out

answer: Winner: Y with 0x0F1 (241), the smallest identifier. X and Z became receivers and read Y's frame without disturbing it.

Second round. When Y's frame and the 3-bit interframe space are over, X and Z start again. X = 001 0010 0011 and Z = 010 1010 0000 agree at bit 10 (0); at bit 9, X sends 0 and Z sends 1, so Z drops out and X (0x123) wins. Z sends last.

answer.text: Timing at 500 kbit/s with 8 data bytes and no stuff bits:
answer.pre:
frame bits incl. interframe space = 44 + 64 + 3 = 111 bits
bit time = 1 ÷ 500 000 = 2 µs  → frame time = 222 µs
Y (0x0F1) ends at 222 µs
X (0x123) ends at 2 × 222 = 444 µs
Z (0x2A0) ends at 3 × 222 = 666 µs

answer: Interpretation. No bus time was wasted and no data lost: the collision was resolved inside the identifier field. The order Y, X, Z is exactly the order of identifiers, so the designer sets priorities by choosing identifiers: the most urgent message gets the smallest number. If Z's message had a 1 ms deadline, it is still met at 666 µs, but under heavier load a high identifier can wait several frames, which is why low identifiers go to safety messages.
Check: 241 < 291 < 672 matches the order Y, X, Z, and the first difference between X and Y is at bit 8 (X has 1, Y has 0), confirming the trace.

bank.q: A 500 kbit/s powertrain CAN bus carries twelve messages: four of 8 data bytes every 10 ms, four of 8 data bytes every 20 ms and four of 4 data bytes every 100 ms. Using worst-case bit stuffing, find the bus load, the worst-case delay of the highest-priority message and of the lowest-priority message, and say what you would do if the load passed 70 per cent.
outline: Worst-case frame bits: 135 for 8 bytes, 95 for 4 bytes
Bus load = Σ bits ÷ period ÷ bit rate
Highest priority: blocking by one lower frame plus its own frame
Lowest priority: all higher frames once plus its own
Remedies: lengthen periods, split bus, CAN FD, higher rate, keep margin

answer.text: Worst-case frame length (standard identifier, interframe space included). Stuff bits are at most (stuffed bits − 1) ÷ 4, rounded down.
answer.pre:
8 bytes: 44 + 64 + 3 = 111 bits; stuffed region 98 → (98 − 1) ÷ 4 = 24 → 135 bits
4 bytes: 44 + 32 + 3 = 79 bits;  stuffed region 66 → (66 − 1) ÷ 4 = 16 → 95 bits
bit time = 2 µs → 8-byte frame 270 µs, 4-byte frame 190 µs

answer.text: Bus load:

answer: U = 84 800 ÷ 500 000 = 0.1696, about 17 per cent. The bus is lightly loaded even with worst-case stuffing.

Worst-case delay of the highest-priority message. Arbitration happens only at the start of a frame, so a frame that becomes ready just after a lower-priority frame has started must wait for it. Worst case: blocking by the longest lower-priority frame (270 µs) plus its own transmission (270 µs) = 540 µs. Nothing of higher priority can delay it.

answer.text: Worst-case delay of the lowest-priority message (a 4-byte, 100 ms message). It suffers no blocking from below, but every higher-priority message ready at the same instant goes first. The total is far below 10 ms, so each higher message is sent at most once in that window:
answer.pre:
higher frames: 8 × 270 µs + 3 × 190 µs = 2160 + 570 = 2730 µs
own frame:     190 µs
worst delay ≈ 2730 + 190 = 2920 µs = 2.92 ms (ignoring error frames)

answer: This is well inside a 100 ms period. Error frames and repeats add to it, so a real analysis adds an error allowance of a few frames.

If the load passed 70 per cent: (1) lengthen the periods of messages that do not need fast updates (moving the 10 ms group to 20 ms halves its 54 000 bit/s); (2) pack more signals into each 8-byte frame to cut overhead, since only 64 of 135 bits are data; (3) move a domain to a second bus behind the gateway; (4) change to CAN FD, whose data phase at 2 Mbit/s and 64-byte payload carry much more per frame; (5) raise the rate to 1 Mbit/s if the bus length allows; (6) always keep a margin (about 30 per cent) for error recovery and new messages.

bank.q: Prepare a bus allocation plan for a car with body, powertrain, chassis and infotainment domains. Choose the bus for each domain, justify each choice with numbers, and show how the domains are coupled.
outline: Work out each domain's data rate and timing need
Body: LIN sub-buses on 125 kbit/s CAN
Powertrain: 500 kbit/s CAN or CAN FD
Chassis and x-by-wire: FlexRay
Infotainment and cameras: MOST or Ethernet, 1000BASE-T1 for raw video
Central gateway, OBD socket, filtering, crossing delay
Cost and wiring arguments
answer: Method. For each domain, find the data rate and the timing need, choose the cheapest bus that meets both with a load margin, then join the buses through a gateway. Draw the plan as a star of buses round a central gateway.

answer.text: Body and comfort. A door module sends 8 frames of 100 bits every 100 ms:
answer.pre:
8 × 100 ÷ 0.100 = 8 000 bit/s = 8 kbit/s → Class A
LIN at 19.2 kbit/s: load 8 ÷ 19.2 = 42 %; 8-byte frame 6.46 ms (max 9.04 ms) fits a 10 ms slot

answer: So each door, seat and climate cluster gets a LIN sub-bus, mastered by a body ECU that sits on a 125 kbit/s body CAN (Class B) with the cluster and lighting. LIN costs least per node and needs one wire.

answer.text: Powertrain. Engine and gearbox exchange 30 messages of 125 bits every 20 ms:

answer: 500 kbit/s high-speed CAN leaves a large margin, gives priority by identifier and is cheap; CAN FD at 2 Mbit/s can be used where calibration and software downloads are large.

Chassis. ABS, ESP and suspension can share a 500 kbit/s CAN, but steer-by-wire or brake-by-wire needs a guaranteed delay and redundancy. FlexRay with a 5 ms cycle gives every static message a worst-case delay of one cycle and two 10 Mbit/s channels, so one broken channel is survived.

answer.text: Infotainment and cameras. A rear camera at 640 × 480 pixels, 16 bits per pixel, 30 pictures per second:
answer.pre:
640 × 480 × 16 × 30 = 147 456 000 bit/s ≈ 147.5 Mbit/s
> 100 Mbit/s → 1000BASE-T1 Ethernet (or compression to fit 100BASE-T1)

answer: Audio and the head unit can use a MOST ring (about 23 Mbit/s, 4 bytes per stereo stream per frame) or 100BASE-T1 Ethernet with AVB; cameras and the backbone use 1000BASE-T1.

answer.text: The plan:

head: Domain
Bus
Rate
Reason
rows: Class B data between body ECUs

answer.text: Coupling. A central gateway joins every bus and the OBD socket; it routes and repacks signals, buffers between rates, blocks infotainment from chassis frames and wakes and sleeps the buses. A powertrain frame copied to the body bus takes

answer: which is acceptable for a cluster display. Check: each bus's load is below about 70 per cent, and the most expensive buses (FlexRay, gigabit Ethernet) are used only where the numbers demand them.

bank.q: A scan tool reads DTC P0301 from a car with the MIL on. The freeze frame gives PID 0C = 25 80, PID 0D = 3E, PID 04 = 59 and PID 05 = 7B. Interpret the code and the freeze frame, explain how the ECU detected the fault and when the lamp came on, and give the steps you would take next.
outline: P0301: powertrain, generic, ignition and misfire, cylinder 1
Decode PIDs with their formulas
Misfire detection from crankshaft speed
Pending code, two-trip rule, MIL; flashing for catalyst-damaging misfire
Diagnosis steps and confirmation of the repair with monitors
answer: Code. P = powertrain; first digit 0 = generic code defined by the standard; second digit 3 = ignition system or misfire; 01 = cylinder 1. P0301 is a misfire detected in cylinder 1. On the bus it is the two bytes 03 01: top bits 00 → P, next 00 → 0, low nibble 3, then 0 and 1.

answer.text: Freeze frame, decoded with the PID formulas:

answer: So the misfire was confirmed with a warm engine (83 °C), at moderate speed and part load: 2400 rpm, 62 km/h, about 35 per cent load. It is not a cold-start problem; it happens under ordinary driving.

answer.text: Detection. The misfire monitor runs continuously. It measures the time between crankshaft teeth: when a cylinder fails to fire, the crank slows during that cylinder's power stroke. For a 4-cylinder engine at 2400 rpm:
answer.pre:
rev time = 60 ÷ 2400 = 25 ms; one power stroke = 180° = 12.5 ms
the ECU compares the speed in each 12.5 ms window and counts slow windows per cylinder

answer: The ECU counts misfires per 200 or 1000 revolutions. When the count passed its limit, it stored a pending code (service 07). Most misfires are two-trip faults: when the fault appeared again in the next drive cycle, the code was confirmed (service 03), the freeze frame above was stored (service 02) and the MIL came on. If the misfire rate is high enough to overheat the catalyst, the MIL flashes at once.

Next steps: (1) read live data and the misfire counters (service 06) to see whether the misfire is still present and only in cylinder 1; (2) swap the cylinder 1 coil (or plug) with cylinder 2; if the code moves to P0302 the coil or plug is faulty; (3) if it stays, check the injector of cylinder 1 (resistance, balance test) and its wiring; (4) if both are good, do a compression or leak-down test for a valve or ring fault; (5) look for a vacuum leak at the cylinder 1 intake runner; (6) repair, clear the codes with service 04, then drive a full drive cycle and check that the misfire monitor reports complete and no pending code returns.

Why not just clear the code: service 04 switches off the lamp and resets the readiness monitors, but the fault returns, and a car with incomplete monitors fails an inspection. Check: 0x2580 = 9600 and 9600 ÷ 4 = 2400 rpm; 0x59 = 89 gives 34.9 per cent, matching the load in the question.

bank.q: Analyse the IEEE 1609 WAVE stack: what 1609.2, 1609.3, 1609.4 and 1609.1 do, how the stack sits on IEEE 802.11p and the DSRC channels, and how much safety traffic one control-channel interval can carry.
outline: DSRC band and channels, the 2020 US change
802.11p PHY: OFDM in 10 MHz, 3 to 27 Mbit/s; MAC: OCB, EDCA, half duplex
1609.2 security, 1609.3 WSMP and IPv6, 1609.4 CCH and SCH switching, 1609.1 resource manager
BSM at 10 Hz; airtime and capacity calculation
Why WSMP and not only IPv6; why channel switching
answer: Radio band. DSRC uses the 5.9 GHz band in 10 MHz channels: in the original US plan 5.850 to 5.925 GHz, with control channel 178 and six service channels. In 2020 the US regulator gave the lower 45 MHz to Wi-Fi and the upper 30 MHz to C-V2X; Europe's ITS-G5 uses the same radio between 5.855 and 5.925 GHz.

802.11p (MAC and PHY). The PHY is 802.11a OFDM with the clock halved: 10 MHz channels, 8 µs symbols and a longer guard time against road echoes and Doppler; rates 3 to 27 Mbit/s, 6 Mbit/s usual for safety. The MAC works outside a basic service set (OCB), with no scanning, association or authentication, so a car can broadcast at once. EDCA gives four access categories so safety frames get shorter waits. The radio is half duplex.

answer.text: WAVE layers above it (draw the stack with 1609.2 as a column beside all layers):

head: Standard
Job
rows: security: signed (and if needed encrypted) messages with PKI certificates; serves every layer
networking: WSMP for short safety messages with a few bytes of header; WAVE service advertisements; IPv6 with UDP or TCP for other traffic
multi-channel operation: a 100 ms sync interval timed by GNSS, normally 50 ms on the control channel and 50 ms on a service channel, with guard times
resource manager for remote applications; little used and later withdrawn

answer: Applications send the basic safety message (BSM, SAE J2735) about 10 times a second: position, speed, heading, acceleration, brake status and size.

answer.text: Capacity of one control-channel interval for 300-byte BSMs at 6 Mbit/s, losing 10 per cent to guard time and contention (preamble and headers ignored):
answer.pre:
bits = 300 × 8 = 2400
airtime = 2400 ÷ 6 000 000 = 0.4 ms
usable CCH = 50 × 0.9 = 45 ms
BSMs = 45 ÷ 0.4 = 112.5 → 112 per interval
one BSM per car per 100 ms → about 112 cars at best
at 3 Mbit/s: airtime 0.8 ms → 56 cars

answer: Analysis 1: why WSMP. An IPv6 + UDP header adds 48 bytes and needs an address; WSMP adds only a few bytes and is broadcast, so a 300-byte BSM stays short. Shorter frames mean more cars per interval, which matters because the capacity above is already near a busy junction's car count.

Analysis 2: why channel switching. A single-radio car can listen to only one channel. If cars chose channels freely, two cars could miss each other's safety messages. 1609.4 makes every car sit on the control channel at the same 50 ms, so safety messages always meet, at the cost of halving the time available for safety traffic. Dual-radio units avoid this by keeping one radio on the safety channel permanently.

Analysis 3: why security sits beside the stack. A signature and certificate add roughly 100 bytes or more to each BSM, which increases airtime; but without 1609.2 a forged "hard braking" message could cause crashes. The design trades capacity for trust.
Conclusion. 802.11p gives a fast, connectionless radio; WAVE adds the timing, short-message networking and security that make it usable for safety. Check: 0.4 ms × 112 = 44.8 ms ≤ 45 ms.

bank.q: Analyse the characteristics and challenges of a VANET: architecture, applications, mobility, road-constrained topology and intermittent links, and explain why position-based routing suits it better than topology-based routing, with calculations.
outline: Ad hoc networks and the three domains
Safety and non-safety applications; road-safety motivation
Characteristics versus MANET
Challenges: link breaks, broadcast storm, GNSS errors, security, privacy
AODV and DSR versus GPSR; greedy and perimeter modes
Contact time and greedy distance calculations
Geocast and store-carry-forward
answer: Architecture. A VANET is an ad hoc network of vehicles: no fixed infrastructure is required and each OBU forwards for others. Three domains: in-vehicle (ECUs and buses joined to the OBU), ad hoc (OBU to OBU and OBU to RSU) and infrastructure (RSU back-haul, internet and servers). Draw the three as nested blocks with an RSU at the boundary.

Applications. Road crashes kill about 1.19 million people a year (WHO, 2023), most in low- and middle-income countries. Safety applications: collision, hazard, intersection and emergency-vehicle warnings. Non-safety: traffic information, tolling, parking and infotainment. Safety messages are short, frequent and urgent; non-safety ones can wait.

Characteristics versus a MANET: high speed, so short links; motion constrained to roads, so predictable; no battery or storage limit; position and time from GNSS; very large and very uneven density (a jam versus an empty highway at night).

answer.text: Link duration with a 300 m radio range:
answer.pre:
oncoming cars, each 100 km/h: closing 200 km/h = 55.6 m/s
contact = 2 × 300 ÷ 55.6 = 600 ÷ 55.6 = 10.8 s
same lane, 100 and 80 km/h: relative 20 km/h = 5.56 m/s
contact from side by side to 300 m apart = 300 ÷ 5.56 = 54 s

answer: Challenges: (1) links break within seconds, especially with oncoming traffic; (2) the broadcast storm when every car rebroadcasts an alert; (3) GNSS errors in tunnels and between tall buildings; (4) fake or replayed messages; (5) tracking of drivers through their messages (privacy).

Topology-based routing. AODV floods a route request, stores the path and repairs it when a link breaks; DSR puts the full path in each packet. With 10 s links on a multi-hop path, a route breaks before or soon after it is found, each repair floods the network again, and packets are lost in between. These protocols are therefore poor for VANETs.

answer.text: Position-based routing (GPSR). Each node knows its neighbours' positions from beacons and the destination's position from a location service; it sends to the neighbour closest to the destination (greedy mode). Example: sender at (0, 0) m, destination (200, 0), neighbours P (80, 40), Q (120, −30), R (60, −10):
answer.pre:
P: √(120² + 40²) = √16 000 = 126.5 m
Q: √(80² + 30²)  = √7 300  = 85.4 m   ← smallest
R: √(140² + 10²) = √19 700 = 140.4 m
sender is 200 m away; Q is closer → forward to Q

answer: If no neighbour is closer than the current node (a void, for example an empty stretch), GPSR switches to perimeter mode: face routing by the right-hand rule on a planarized graph of the radio neighbours, until a node closer than the void is reached; delivery is guaranteed only if that graph is connected. No route is stored, so a broken link costs nothing; the next hop is chosen afresh from current positions.

Supporting techniques: geocast to every car in a zone, with only the farthest receiver rebroadcasting to stop the storm; store-carry-forward, where a car carries the packet until another car or an RSU comes in range.

Conclusion: because VANET links are short-lived but positions are known and road-bound, routing by position with local decisions beats routing by stored paths. Check: 85.4 < 126.5 < 140.4, and 600 ÷ 55.6 = 10.8 s.

bank.q: Evaluate whether DSRC (IEEE 802.11p) or cellular V2X is the better choice for intersection warnings in Indian mixed traffic, with latency and channel-load numbers.
outline: The two radio families and their direct modes
Latency budget and warning distance
Channel load at a busy junction
Mixed traffic: two-wheelers and pedestrians need V2P
Infrastructure cost, spectrum and phone penetration
Security in both
Verdict with conditions
answer: The options. DSRC uses IEEE 802.11p at 5.9 GHz: ad hoc, no SIM or tower, mature, but it needs roadside units (RSUs) for V2I. Cellular V2X (LTE-V2X, now 5G NR-V2X) has a direct sidelink (PC5) for V2V, V2I and V2P without a tower, plus the normal network link (V2N) to the cloud.

answer.text: Latency matters only through the warning distance. A car and a two-wheeler close at 20 m/s on a blind junction and the rider needs 2 s:

answer: Either latency is acceptable for this warning, so both direct modes (802.11p and C-V2X sidelink) qualify; a path through the cloud is slower and fails without coverage, so it should not carry the safety warning itself.

answer.text: Channel load. A busy junction has 150 vehicles within range, each sending a 300-byte BSM 10 times a second at 6 Mbit/s (0.4 ms each):
answer.pre:
airtime per second = 150 × 10 × 0.4 ms = 600 ms → 60 % of a channel used full time
with 1609.4 switching, CCH has 45 ms usable per 100 ms → 112 BSMs, but 150 are needed → overload

answer: So in Indian traffic density either radio needs congestion control: lower message rates for slow vehicles, power control, or a dedicated safety channel all the time. C-V2X's scheduled resource selection copes somewhat better with dense traffic, while 802.11p with dual radios avoids the channel-switching loss.

Mixed traffic. Two-wheelers, auto-rickshaws and pedestrians are a large share of road users and of deaths. A phone-based V2P app is far easier with C-V2X, because phones already have cellular radios; 802.11p radios are not in phones.

Deployment and cost. 802.11p needs RSUs at each junction to be useful for V2I, paid for by road authorities; C-V2X can reuse towers for V2N and add RSUs only where needed. Spectrum: the US moved its 5.9 GHz V2X band to C-V2X in 2020, so global industry momentum is with C-V2X; India has to allocate a band for either.
Security. Both use signed messages with certificates; both need a PKI and revocation. This does not separate them.

answer.text: Evaluation:

answer: Verdict. For Indian intersection warnings, cellular V2X is the better long-term choice, because it reaches phones (V2P) and reuses towers, and its sidelink gives the same direct, low-latency link as DSRC; but the safety warning must use the direct mode, not the network, and both systems need congestion control at the 150-vehicle level calculated above. A hybrid is likely: direct links for safety and the network for cloud services. Check: 150 × 10 × 0.4 ms = 600 ms per second.

bank.q: A steer-by-wire system must meet ASIL D and runs on FlexRay. Evaluate how the ISO 26262 lifecycle, MISRA C coding and FlexRay together provide the safety evidence, with an ASIL determination, an FTTI budget and a hardware-metric check.
outline: HARA: S3, E4, C3 → ASIL D
Safety goal and safety concept: redundancy, plausibility, safe state
FTTI budget with FlexRay cycle times
SPFM for ASIL D
MISRA C and tool qualification as software evidence
FlexRay's role: static slots, two channels, bus guardian behaviour
Limits and verdict
answer: HARA. Hazard: unintended or lost steering at motorway speed. Severity S3 (life-threatening), exposure E4 (every drive), controllability C3 (a driver cannot control a sudden steer). S + E + C = 3 + 4 + 3 = 10, so ASIL D. Safety goal: "no unintended steering torque and no loss of steering" (ASIL D).

Safety concept. Two independent angle sensors and two controllers compare values (plausibility); the actuator motor has two windings and two drivers; a watchdog checks each controller; every steering message carries end-to-end protection (counter and CRC); the safe state is a degraded mode on the healthy channel with a warning. ASIL decomposition can give each channel ASIL B(D) if their independence (separate power, sensors, timing) is shown.

answer.text: FTTI budget. Suppose the FTTI is 50 ms. FlexRay cycle 5 ms; each controller needs two cycles to confirm a fault:
answer.pre:
sensor sampling and transfer (1 cycle)   5 ms
confirmation (2 cycles)                 10 ms
detection and switch-over logic         15 ms
actuator to degraded mode               20 ms
total = 5 + 10 + 15 + 20 = 50 ms = FTTI → just met; no margin

answer: Evaluation: with no margin, the design should shorten the cycle to 2.5 ms (saving 7.5 ms on sampling and confirmation) or make the actuator switch faster. On CAN the same budget could not be proven, because a frame can wait behind higher-priority frames and repeated errors; on FlexRay a static slot arrives every cycle on both channels, so the 5 ms sampling term is guaranteed.

answer.text: Hardware metric. ASIL D requires SPFM ≥ 99 per cent. Example: total rate λ = 400 FIT, single-point faults 1 FIT, residual faults 2 FIT:

answer: If a sensor without diagnostics added 2 FIT of single-point faults, SPFM would fall to 1 − 5 ÷ 400 = 98.75 per cent and fail; better diagnostic coverage or redundancy would be needed.

MISRA C. The steering software is written to MISRA C:2012: no recursion (stack bounded), no heap (Rule 21.3), no value-losing conversions, braces and default cases everywhere, checked returns. A qualified static analyser proves compliance, and every deviation is documented. This supports ISO 26262 part 6 by making the code analysable and its timing predictable, which the FTTI argument needs. Tools such as the compiler and code generator must be qualified.

What each part proves: ISO 26262 provides the structure (HARA, safety goal, concept, metrics, verification, safety case and independent assessment); FlexRay provides the timing and communication redundancy; MISRA C provides code-level evidence. None is sufficient alone: MISRA code on CAN without a timing proof fails the FTTI argument, and FlexRay with badly written code can still fail.

Verdict. The combination can support an ASIL D claim, provided the FTTI margin is increased, the SPFM stays above 99 per cent and the independence of the two channels is demonstrated. Check: 3 + 4 + 3 = 10, 5 + 10 + 15 + 20 = 50 ms and 1 − 3/400 = 99.25 per cent.

glossary.def: A single shared medium on which several nodes exchange messages.
Any device on a network that can send or receive, such as an ECU or the diagnostic socket.
Electronic control unit: a small computer that reads sensors, drives actuators and talks on the bus.
One quantity, such as engine speed, carried inside a message; one message usually holds several signals.
Sending many signals over one medium in turn, instead of one wire per signal.
An ECU that joins buses of different protocols and decides which signals cross, up to OSI layer 7.
A device that joins two segments of the same protocol at the data link layer.
A guarantee that the worst-case message delay is known in advance.
The fraction of time a bus is busy carrying frames.
The wiring shape of a network: bus, star, ring, daisy chain or a hybrid.
Time-division multiple access: each node owns fixed time slots.
Carrier sense multiple access: a node sends when it finds the medium idle.
A seven-layer model of communication, from the physical layer to the application layer.
The transport protocol (ISO 15765-2) that cuts long diagnostic messages into CAN frames.
The CAN logic 0, which overrides a recessive bit on the bus.
The CAN logic 1, the idle level that any dominant bit overrides.
The bit-wise contest at the start of a CAN frame that the lowest identifier wins.
Adding one opposite bit after five equal bits so that receivers stay synchronised.
The CAN state of a node whose transmit error counter has passed 255; it stops sending.
CAN with a faster data phase and up to 64 data bytes, keeping CAN's arbitration.
Local Interconnect Network: a single-wire master-slave bus up to 20 kbit/s for body modules.
The LIN master's fixed list of frames and their time slots.
A dual-channel, time-triggered bus at 10 Mbit/s per channel for chassis and x-by-wire systems.
A short time unit of the FlexRay dynamic segment that a node stretches when it sends.
Switched Ethernet on one twisted pair (100BASE-T1, 1000BASE-T1) for cameras and backbones.
Media Oriented Systems Transport: a synchronous ring, often optical, for audio, video and infotainment.
The MOST device that generates the frames and the clock for the whole ring.
The standard 16-pin socket, protocols, services and fault codes for emissions diagnostics.
Parameter identifier: the number of one live value in OBD-II service 01.
Diagnostic trouble code: a letter and four digits naming a fault.
Malfunction indicator lamp, the engine warning lamp lit for confirmed emissions faults.
Coding guidelines that remove risky constructs from embedded C.
Automotive safety integrity level, A (lowest) to D (highest), from hazard analysis.
Fault tolerant time interval: the minimum time from a fault to a possible hazardous event.
Vehicle-to-everything radio communication: V2V, V2I, V2P, V2N and V2G.
On-board unit (the V2X radio in a car) and roadside unit (a fixed V2X radio).
Vehicular ad hoc network: a wireless network formed by moving vehicles.
Dedicated short-range communications, the 5.9 GHz radio service for road safety.
Wireless access in vehicular environments, the IEEE 1609 layers above 802.11p.
Basic safety message: position, speed, heading and braking, sent about ten times a second.
